name: Deindividuation
aliases: Loss of self in the crowd
statement: Submerged in a crowd and stripped of identity, people do things they never would alone.
statementAccent: people do things they never would alone
meaning: Deindividuation is a concept in social psychology describing a psychological state in which individuals in groups or crowds experience a loss of self-awareness and individual identity, along with a reduced sense of personal accountability, leading to disinhibited behaviour they would not engage in alone. Such behaviour is often impulsive and antinormative, and can be antisocial, as in mob violence and riots. The term was coined by Leon Festinger, Albert Pepitone, and Theodore Newcomb in 1952, building on Gustave Le Bon's nineteenth-century crowd psychology, set out in his 1895 book The Crowd, which held that individuals in a crowd become dominated by a collective, irrational mindset. Philip Zimbardo later developed the theory, identifying factors such as anonymity, arousal, and sensory overload that promote the state. Deindividuation offers a framework for understanding how the anonymity and immersion of crowds, uniforms, and online settings can loosen the restraints that normally govern individual conduct.
mechanism: The classic account holds that immersion in a group reduces self-awareness and the sense of being personally identifiable and accountable, which lowers the internal restraints, conscience, guilt, fear of judgment, that normally regulate behaviour. Attention shifts outward from one's own values toward situational and group cues, so people become more responsive to the crowd's norms and the immediate environment than to their personal standards. Factors that promote deindividuation include anonymity, through masks, uniforms, darkness, large crowds, or online settings; diffusion of responsibility; group size and immersion; heightened arousal; and altered states. A modern reinterpretation, the social identity model of deindividuation effects, developed by Reicher, Spears, and Postmes, reframes the process: rather than a mindless loss of all identity, deindividuation involves a shift from personal identity to a salient social identity, so behaviour conforms to the norms of the relevant group, which may be prosocial or antisocial depending on those norms. On this view crowds are not simply unrestrained but governed by group standards.

examples.text: Anonymity from masks, uniforms, darkness, or a large crowd reduces the sense of being identifiable, loosening restraints on behaviour.
The anonymity of online settings can produce deindividuated behaviour such as trolling, as people act without the accountability of a visible identity.
The social identity model recasts deindividuation as a shift to group identity, so a crowd's behaviour follows its norms, which can be prosocial or antisocial.

variants.name: Classic deindividuation theory
variants.text: The original account in which anonymity and immersion reduce self-awareness and accountability, releasing impulsive, antinormative behaviour.

variants.name: The SIDE model
variants.text: The social identity model of deindividuation effects, holding that the state shifts people from personal to social identity, so behaviour follows group norms.

whyItMatters: Deindividuation is a foundational concept for understanding collective behaviour, from riots and mob violence to online disinhibition, uniformed conduct, and the dynamics of cults and gangs. It captures how the anonymity and immersion of group settings can loosen the personal restraints that ordinarily govern behaviour, helping explain why people in crowds may act in ways they would find unthinkable alone. Its intellectual history, from Le Bon's crowd psychology through the classic theory to the modern social identity model, tracks a shift in how psychologists conceive of collective action: not as a mindless dissolution of the self but often as a change in which identity is salient. That reframing matters because it implies crowd behaviour follows group norms and can be prosocial as well as destructive, with implications for policing, protest, and the design of online spaces.

working.text: place a person in a crowd or anonymous setting that reduces self-awareness and the sense of being individually identifiable.
note that reduced accountability weakens the conscience and fear of judgment that normally regulate behaviour.
expect behaviour to track the crowd's cues and norms, which the social identity model frames as a shift to group identity.

limits: Deindividuation is an influential but contested framework, and its classic form has been criticised. Anonymity and group immersion do not always produce antisocial behaviour; the social identity model argues that outcomes depend on the norms of the salient group, which can be prosocial, so deindividuation is not inherently a slide into aggression. Some evidence often cited for the theory, such as the Stanford Prison Experiment, has been heavily criticised on methodological and ethical grounds, and specific figures from studies like the Halloween trick-or-treater research come from secondary summaries. The concept overlaps with related processes like diffusion of responsibility and conformity. So deindividuation captures a real and important pattern in collective behaviour, but its mechanisms and predictions remain debated, with the social identity account now the leading refinement.
misreadings: Deindividuation does not mean people in crowds inevitably become violent; whether behaviour turns antisocial depends on the norms of the group, and crowds can act prosocially. It is not simply a total loss of all identity, at least on the modern view, but a shift from personal to social identity, so conduct follows group standards rather than dissolving into chaos. And it is not established by the most dramatic cases; some celebrated evidence, like the Stanford Prison Experiment, is methodologically disputed, so treating deindividuation as a proven cause of mob evil overstates a real but debated phenomenon.
origin: Coined by Leon Festinger, Albert Pepitone, and Theodore Newcomb in 1952, building on Gustave Le Bon's 1895 crowd psychology, later developed by Philip Zimbardo and reframed by the social identity model of Reicher, Spears, and Postmes.
